title: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN) — section 1
text:
NATIONAL STRATEGY

ON THE RESILIENCE OF CRITICAL ENTITIES

Securing critical infrastructure is a matter of national interest. In an era of increasingly complex challenges marked by global uncertainty, climate change, pandemic risks, conflict, and hybrid threats, it is the duty of the State to protect the essential services that underpin daily life: energy, transport, communications, health, water, food security, and financial stability.

This National Strategy on the Resilience of Critical Entities is the result of extensive collaboration between institutions, competent authorities, the scientific community and businesses. More than just a technical roadmap,

it sets out a clear vision: to enhance Italy’s resilience and self-reliance, safeguard the public interest, and establish a robust protective network for our essential services.

This Strategy implements Legislative Decree No. 134 of 2024, transposing the EU Critical Entities Resilience (CER) Directive into national law. Alongside the National Cybersecurity Strategy, it forms part of a broader proactive European effort to tackle systemic vulnerabilities with determination during unpredictable times.

By fostering public-privat
standard: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN)

title: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN) — section 2
text:
t of a broader proactive European effort to tackle systemic vulnerabilities with determination during unpredictable times.

By fostering public-private partnerships and leveraging both existing expertise and new skills, the Strategy aims to prevent risks and enhance national preparedness, moving beyond improvisation in the protection of essential services with clear and responsible method and vision.

The Government recognises that resilience cannot be built in isolation. It is a shared endeavour that brings together institutions, businesses, citizens, and research facilities, because for a nation to be strong, it must be cohesive, one in which every stakeholder contributes to the common good.

This Strategy marks a decisive step towards achieving that goal, by providing the framework to secure a safer, more stable future of greater freedom.

The National Strategy on the Resilience of Critical Entities is aimed at public and private entities providing essential services which, if disrupted, would significantly impact the maintenance of vital societal functions, economic activities, public health and safety, or the environment. These entities are identified as the operators of criti
standard: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN)

title: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN) — section 3
text: f vital societal functions, economic activities, public health and safety, or the environment. These entities are identified as the operators of critical infrastructure – comprising the networks, facilities, systems or devices indispensable for service continuity – which must be protected and made resilient against physical events that could jeopardise their operation. Drafted pursuant to Article 6 of Legislative Decree No. 134 of 4 September 2024, which transposes Directive (EU) 2022/2557 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 December 2022 on the resilience of critical entities (also known as the “CER – Critical Entities Resilience – Directive”) into Italian law, the Strategy seeks to enhance the prevention, response and recovery capacities of critical entities, especially by protecting the infrastructure required to ensure operational continuity in the event of physical incidents. While focused on physical risk, within the scope of the CER Directive, the Strategy recognises that widespread disruption or damage, in the current landscape, often stems from hybrid campaigns - hostile threats or actions designed to undermine infrastructure, essential services, and decisi
standard: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN)

title: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN) — section 4
text:
current landscape, often stems from hybrid campaigns - hostile threats or actions designed to undermine infrastructure, essential services, and decision- making processes.

The ability of critical infrastructure to provide essential services to the population can be impacted by climate change, cross-border and cross-sectoral interdependencies, the spread of digital technology and geopolitical events. Added to this are the deliberate actions of hostile actors, who aim to amplify existing vulnerabilities through hybrid means, including information, cyber, economic and physical pressure. This complex scenario requires a resilience-oriented approach to safeguard the well-being of the population and the economic competitiveness and security of the country, which can be achieved through close cooperation among the public and private entities involved in the management, control, and protection of infrastructure, in various capacities.

Critical infrastructure is a cornerstone of numerous Union initiatives, including, in chronological order, the Niinistö Report, the White Paper on European Defence Readiness 2030, and the European Preparedness Union Strategy. These frameworks advocate for a
standard: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN)

title: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN) — section 5
text:
the Niinistö Report, the White Paper on European Defence Readiness 2030, and the European Preparedness Union Strategy. These frameworks advocate for an integrated all-hazards, whole-of- government and whole-of-society approach.

It is therefore necessary to:

apply resilience principles to existing critical infrastructure to mitigate vulnerabilities, supported by an analysis of preventive measures and available instruments; and

ensure that new infrastructure is developed according to resilience-by-design principles, also on the basis of assessments by the Ministry of Defence, extending the established methodology for dual-use systems. National defence and military security assessments should form one of the pillars of critical infrastructure development, providing for a strategy to implement protective measures throughout the entire infrastructure lifecycle.

This document defines strategic objectives and priorities to strengthen the resilience of Italian critical entities seeking to forge synergies with existing policy frameworks, notably the National Cybersecurity Strategy 2022–2026. Given the intrinsic link between the overall resilience of critical entities and their cybersecu
standard: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN)

title: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN) — section 6
text:
otably the National Cybersecurity Strategy 2022–2026. Given the intrinsic link between the overall resilience of critical entities and their cybersecurity, effective institutional coordination at the operational level is an essential factor, since it addresses key areas such as:

the exchange of information on risks and incidents,

the execution of coordinated oversight activities for entities within both the CER and NIS2 frameworks,

the harmonised interpretation of compliance obligations, to avoid the risk of disproportionate burdens or contradictory guidance for operators.

The involvement of the private sector in the national resilience strategy for critical entities is a structural necessity rather than an option. In Italy, most of the infrastructure providing essential services – spanning the energy, communications, transport, and finance sectors – is owned or operated by private entities. Establishing strategic, continuous, and structured forms of public- private collaboration is therefore essential to effectively address any challenges to resilience.

Furthermore, the public administration – recognised, under Legislative Decree No. 134 of 2024, as a critical sector – serves
standard: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN)

title: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN) — section 7
text:
hallenges to resilience.

Furthermore, the public administration – recognised, under Legislative Decree No. 134 of 2024, as a critical sector – serves as a fundamental enabler of the functioning of the national system as a whole. The operational continuity of essential public services and the robustness of administrative capacity are prerequisites for ensuring efficient and reliable service provision and play a vital role in minimising disruptions to citizens and businesses, and, ultimately, in strengthening the overall resilience of other strategic sectors.

THE GEOPOLITICAL CONTEXT

AND RISKS

The current policy landscape is defined by escalating complexity and uncertainty, propelled by intensified competition among state actors, persistent threats from non-state actors, and the challenges arising as a result of economic, socio-political, demographic, environmental and technological trends. Further drivers of instability are emerging within this context, alongside a highly dynamic international environment polarised by ongoing conflicts, including social shifts (such as demographic change, migration and urbanisation), economic vulnerabilities (due to increased downside risks and
standard: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN)

title: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN) — section 8
text:
icts, including social shifts (such as demographic change, migration and urbanisation), economic vulnerabilities (due to increased downside risks and competition for resources), environmental threats (climate change, emergencies and natural disasters), and technological risks (space competition, advanced technology dependence, vulnerability of digital infrastructure, cyberspace, and the pervasive nature of information). The interplay of all these factors creates a multifaceted stratification of systemic uncertainty and instability.

Critical infrastructure operators find themselves operating within an environment defined by a broad, diverse, and constantly evolving risk landscape consisting of:

Natural risks (seismic, volcanic, hydrogeological, meteorological risks, water scarcity, fires, pandemics): The increasing frequency and magnitude of these events requires the development of adaptation strategies to enhance the physical resilience of exposed infrastructure and systems.

Man-made risks: Stemming from both intentional and accidental actions, these risks underscore the importance of promoting a robust safety culture, continuous staff training, and thorough operational procedur
standard: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN)

title: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN) — section 9
text:
ntal actions, these risks underscore the importance of promoting a robust safety culture, continuous staff training, and thorough operational procedures for essential service operators. This includes implementing effective physical protection measures and performing a detailed analysis of organisational factors – such as human error – and conducting background checks.

Cross-sectoral and cross-border risks: These risks reflect the interdependencies between networks and critical functions, as well as between different sectors, which are exacerbated by high levels of complexity and interconnectedness. Such vulnerabilities can hinder the isolation and containment of malfunctions, both within and across sectors, and delay the timely identification of critical issues and the formulation of effective responses. In this context, supply chain disruptions require a reassessment of risk management strategies, prioritising the mapping of critical physical and digital chains.

These risk categories do not manifest in isolation but are increasingly interconnected, creating complex scenarios where a single event can trigger or amplify other disruptive effects.

Public administration entities are
standard: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN)

y interconnected, creating complex scenarios where a single event can trigger or amplify other disruptive effects.

Public administration entities are also directly exposed to natural and man-made risks – whether accidental or malicious – and to challenges such as skills shortages. Furthermore, they face indirect consequences stemming from knock-on effects triggered by disruptive events, in sectors such as energy, digital infrastructure, and transport. These events may originate in either physical or cyber

environments and the resulting vulnerabilities can jeopardise the provision of essential public services, resulting in significant impacts on citizens and businesses.

The interplay between risks, vulnerabilities, interdependencies, and the amplification of effects has led to the identification of three strategic objectives, which apply both to public administration entities and the institutions responsible for coordination, guidance and oversight, and to the public and private entities operating critical infrastructure.

Legislative Decree No. 134 of 2024 repealed Legislative Decree No. 61 of 2011, introducing updated provisions in the Italian legal system for identifying criti

title: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN) — section 11
text:
ve Decree No. 134 of 2024 repealed Legislative Decree No. 61 of 2011, introducing updated provisions in the Italian legal system for identifying critical entities, their physical resilience obligations, and the related penalties. It further designates the national competent authorities and establishes the relevant National Strategy. Simultaneously, Legislative Decree No. 138 of 2024 transposed Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (known as the “NIS2 Directive”), which mandates a high common level of cybersecurity across the Union. For the banking and financial market infrastructure sectors, the regulatory framework is governed by Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 on digital operational resilience (the Digital Operational Resilience Act or DORA), which contains special provisions for the resilience aspects governed by the CER Directive.

The national resilience of critical entities relies on the active collaboration of diverse public and private stakeholders, and is structured around a multi-level approach involving national institutions and sector-specific competent authorities.

The national architecture defines the responsible authorities, building on existing structures and expertise to enhance the
standard: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN)

ic competent authorities.

The national architecture defines the responsible authorities, building on existing structures and expertise to enhance the resilience of critical entities. The key actors within this framework include:

President of the Council of Ministers (Prime Minister): Tasked with ensuring unified strategic leadership and direction, exercising senior management functions, governmental guidance, and policy coordination in respect of the resilience of critical entities.

Interministerial Committee for Resilience (CIR): Established within the Presidency of the Council of Ministers, the CIR supports the high-level management tasks assigned to the President of the Council of Ministers. Its composition integrates the technical expertise of sector-specific authorities with the functional expertise required to achieve general resilience objectives.

Sectoral Competent Authorities (ASC): These authorities are responsible for correctly applying the provisions of the decree within their respective sectors. They are designated based on their jurisdiction over the sectors and subsectors referred to in the legislation. Each authority is responsible for a specific critical sector
standard: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN)

title: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN) — section 14

sectors, monitoring compliance with regulatory obligations, receiving and managing incident notifications, and have the power to impose penalties in the event of non-compliance with the relevant provisions.

Single Point of Contact (SPC): Established within the Presidency of the Council of Ministers, the SPC role is held by the Military Adviser to the President of the Council of Ministers, supported by the Critical Infrastructure Office within the General Secretariat of the Presidency. The SPC is responsible for facilitating cooperation between national competent authorities and liaising with the European Commission, other Member States, and third countries. Its duties include receiving incident notifications from critical entities and communicating relevant information, where necessary, to the European Commission and the SPCs of other Member States.

National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN): As the top cybersecurity authority, the ACN is responsible for the cyber resilience of critical entities. It collaborates with the Sectoral Competent Authorities (ASCs) to manage cyber threats, share cyber incident data, and implement preventive measures for digital infrastructure protection. In t

t Authorities (ASCs) to manage cyber threats, share cyber incident data, and implement preventive measures for digital infrastructure protection. In this capacity, the ACN operates in a twofold capacity, by involving the Cybersecurity Nucleus (NCS), as the national authority responsible for cybersecurity pursuant to Decree-Law No. 82 of 2021, and as the competent national NIS authority and NIS single point of contact pursuant to Legislative Decree No. 138 of 2024. It also designates the ACN (with coordinating functions) and the Ministry of Defence as the national authorities responsible for cyber crisis management.

The framework further sets out specific obligations and responsibilities for the:

Sectoral Competent Authorities (ASCs): Which are required to carry out risk assessments within their respective remits, contribute to the national risk assessment effort, and perform supervisory functions over the critical entities within their jurisdiction;

Critical Entities: Which are required to establish an appropriate internal organisation and adopt proportionate resilience-boosting technical, security, and organisational measures. These measures must be documented in a comprehensiv

tion and adopt proportionate resilience-boosting technical, security, and organisational measures. These measures must be documented in a comprehensive resilience plan.

The SPC and the ASCs collaborate with the European Commission and other Member States to promote coordinated resilience policies, facilitate joint actions with third countries, and foster the exchange of information, best practices and common methodologies to enhance the resilience of critical entities.

In this context, the Security Intelligence Agencies – responsible for monitoring and countering threats to national security – provide the various components of the national architecture with the intelligence and assessment frameworks they need to enhance the resilience of critical infrastructure. They contribute to the effective implementation of the Strategy’s measures and report on their activities and involvement, in accordance with the procedures established by Law No 124 of  2007.

The Ministry of Defence, within its mandate for national defence and military security, provides the national resilience framework with a strategic and operational policy steer. Combined with the ensuing implications, this is aimed

urity, provides the national resilience framework with a strategic and operational policy steer. Combined with the ensuing implications, this is aimed at enhancing the resilience of critical infrastructure and ensuring the effective implementation of this Strategy. Recognising that any incident, isolated or otherwise, affecting strategic infrastructure – ranging from the severing of a submarine cable or a power outage to disruptions in transport and information services – may be part of a coordinated hybrid campaign, the Ministry independently assesses the need for technical and operational support. This includes executing strategic vulnerability assessments, developing stress-testing indicators and methodologies, and undertaking any other essential initiative capable of safeguarding national resilience, according to the procedures and timelines determined by the specific nature of the threats and the strategic importance of the sectors involved, and acting in coordination with the sectoral competent authorities and consistently with their respective mandates, as defined by Legislative Decree No. 134 of 4 September 2024, ensuring that their specific expertise is fully leveraged.

The cross-cutting nature of resilience requires structured coordination among the relevant public institutions to ensure effective, synergistic, and sustainable action, while minimising overlaps and inconsistencies.

This function is exercised by the SPC, primarily in conjunction with the ASCs and the other bodies of the Presidency of the Council of Ministers involved in the protection of critical infrastructure, which include the Civil Protection Department for matters related to emergency management, and the General Secretariat for the implementation of the Golden Power   legislation.

For civil defence matters – including scenarios impacting the operation of state offices across the country and territorial cohesion, as referred to in Article 14 of Legislative Decree No. 300 of 30 July 1999 – the SPC coordinates with the Interministerial Technical Commission for Civil Defence at the Ministry of the Interior and activates the network of Prefectures (Government Territorial Offices).

The coordination effort also involves the ACN, given

The coordination effort also involves the ACN, given its dual role as the ASC for digital infrastructure and the Competent Authority and Single Point of Contact for the implementation of the NIS2 Directive. This collaboration is both a regulatory requirement and a response to the increasingly integrated and cyber-physical nature of critical infrastructure, which makes the integration of physical resilience and cybersecurity an essential factor.

Cooperation between the SPC and the ACN, as well as among the various NIS competent authorities, establishes a robust framework for effective and synergistic collaboration. In this general context, exchanging information is the cornerstone for shared analyses and ensuring a coordinated response between the ASCs, the SPC, the ACN, and other public administration entities responsible for resilience and national defence and military security matters.

MEASURES TO SUPPORT CRITICAL

ENTITIES

The in-depth knowledge of critical infrastructure by its operators, combined with the public sector’s overall technical and regulatory expertise, is a prerequisite for making comprehensive integrated risk assessments. While private operators possess an operational understanding of vulnerabilities and the potential impact of disruptions or incidents, public authorities have the capacity to analyse and assess risks, whether natural, accidental or intentional. Only strategic and structured public-private collaboration can ensure a holistic risk analysis and the identification of effective strategies to enhance the resilience of the national system.

To this end, the SPC and the ASCs will facilitate public-private cooperation through:

The timely and bi-directional exchange of
standard: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN)

Measure 3.4: Establishes a permanent collaboration channel with the Italian Association of Corporate Security Professionals (AIPSA), as the representative body of the chief security officers of leading Italian enterprises, which includes sharing findings from major accidents (according to Measure 1.4) to develop “lessons learnt” for the benefit of the entire critical entity community.

Public-private synergy constitutes an essential strategic asset for effectively addressing systemic risks – particularly those of a hybrid and emerging nature – thereby structurally enhancing the country’s resilience.

OVERVIEW OF THE NATIONAL RISK ASSESSMENT

The SPC, in collaboration with the ASCs and other institutional bodies, has conducted the Member State risk assessment, incorporating the findings of the national risk assessment, an evaluation required under the EU civil protection mechanism, as well as other relevant assessments carried out according to the national and EU provisions. Furthermore, the findings of the aggregate risk analysis conducted by the AIPSA were integr
standard: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN)

title: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN) — section 28
text:
s carried out according to the national and EU provisions. Furthermore, the findings of the aggregate risk analysis conducted by the AIPSA were integrated into the framework.

The analysis adopted a systemic approach, designed to assess the overall exposure of the diverse sectors to specific risk categories, in terms of their resilience and operational continuity, moving beyond the localised effects of disruptive events on individual infrastructures or components.

The assessment was conducted in three phases:

Risk identification and classification: To map the exposure of each sector and subsector under the decree to a range of natural, technological and man-made events (both accidental and malicious).

Vulnerability analysis: To identify the weaknesses across the various subsectors, taking into account both structural and systemic factors.

Potential impact assessment: To evaluate the systemic effects of disruptions within a sector, in terms of their impact on public health and safety, societal well-being, the economy and the functioning of the EU internal market.

The methodology involved assigning an overall risk level – none, low, medium, medium-high, high – to each subsector
standard: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN)

title: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN) — section 29
text:
oning of the EU internal market.

The methodology involved assigning an overall risk level – none, low, medium, medium-high, high – to each subsector across different risk categories, resulting from the interaction between the potential severity of the damage and the probability of occurrence of a disruptive event.

At this stage, the assessment focused on the so-called “inherent risk” – as the intrinsic risk level associated with specific sectors and subsectors – evaluating the risk to which each sector and subsector is exposed by virtue of its fundamental nature, independently of any existing or planned prevention, control, or mitigation measures.

Regarding risk identification and classification, a wide range of categories was mapped for every sector and subsector defined in the decree, such as natural, technological, anthropogenic, cross- sectoral, and cross-border risks.

This framework provided a comprehensive overview of the risk landscape. Weaknesses within the various subsectors were also examined, as part of the vulnerability analysis, in relation to the identified risks. Vulnerabilities are not limited to physical or structural exposure, but also account for:

Cross-sect
standard: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN)

title: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN) — section 31
text:
ue to interdependencies, particularly regarding the energy, telecommunications and transport sectors. Similar critical issues affect specific supply chains, which are classified as high-risk due to their international dimension.

Furthermore, the human factor remains a significant area of concern, specifically regarding the shortage of highly specialised personnel. This is particularly acute within the public administration, a sector that requires a revision of recruitment standards to attract and retain such specialised professionals.

Natural hazards, such as earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and tsunamis, are generally classified as medium or medium-low risk, with some regional  exceptions.

The outlook differs for hydrogeological and hydraulic risks, which are classified as high-risk for most sectors, primarily due to the increasing frequency of extreme weather events. Furthermore, numerous regions are vulnerable to water scarcity resulting from prolonged  droughts.

Certain sectors face medium-high risks associated with aging infrastructure. Finally, while less frequent, the threats of sabotage and terrorism nevertheless remain significant. Hybrid threats — which operate across
standard: IT National Resilience Strategy — Critical Entities (EN)

text:
astructure. Finally, while less frequent, the threats of sabotage and terrorism nevertheless remain significant. Hybrid threats — which operate across multiple domains by combining cyberattacks, physical sabotage, and disinformation, among other things — further complicate crisis management and preparedness and institutional response.

Following is an overview of the primary findings by sector.

Energy – Electricity subsector: The most critical natural hazards affecting electricity generation and transmission are extreme weather events and water scarcity. Standard hydrogeological and meteorological events are classified as medium risk. For the distribution network, natural risks are generally less significant. Man-made risks are typically low, with the exception of the renewable energy sector, which exhibits high vulnerability to unlawful interference and a significant risk of criminal infiltration. The subsector’s primary vulnerabilities stem from a heavy reliance on other critical infrastructure – particularly digital networks – and on foreign supplies.

Energy – Gas subsector: Fires represent the most critical natural risk, assessed as medium-high, followed by hydraulic and hydr

text:
on foreign supplies.

Energy – Gas subsector: Fires represent the most critical natural risk, assessed as medium-high, followed by hydraulic and hydrogeological hazards, which are classified as medium. Man-made risks, including acts of terrorism and sabotage, are considered high. There is medium-to-high concern regarding cross-border incidents, driven by significant dependencies on third-country entities and international supply chains.

Energy – Other subsectors: Natural risks are generally low, except in district heating and cooling, where seismic hazards and water scarcity play a significant role. In the oil sector, there is a medium-level risk of sabotage, alongside a critical vulnerability linked to strong interdependencies with the transport sector.

Transport – Aviation subsector: Natural hazards such as tsunamis, hydraulic, and hydrogeological risks are classified as medium-high, while extreme weather events are considered high-risk. The risk associated with terrorist threats and sabotage is high. A significant risk also stems from the structural deterioration of infrastructure if scheduled maintenance is not consistently performed. The risk of cross-border incidents is me

s from the structural deterioration of infrastructure if scheduled maintenance is not consistently performed. The risk of cross-border incidents is medium-high. Primary vulnerabilities

arise from cross-sectoral interdependencies, particularly with the energy, telecommunications, and other transport  sectors.

Transport – Rail subsector: Hydrogeological and hydraulic hazards are classified as high-risk, while seismic and extreme weather events are medium-high. Although vandalism, sabotage, and thefts of critical components are the most frequent threats, the strategic nature of rail services results in a medium-high to high risk assessment for terrorist or hybrid threats. The sector exhibits high interdependency with the energy, telecommunications, and intermodal transport sectors and is vulnerable due to its reliance on imports of essential maintenance materials and components.

Transport – Maritime subsector: Natural hazards are generally low, with the exception of extreme weather events, which are assessed as medium. The sector remains a potential target for terrorist or hybrid attacks. Principal concerns involve cross-sectoral risks – specifically dependencies on energy, telecom

ins a potential target for terrorist or hybrid attacks. Principal concerns involve cross-sectoral risks – specifically dependencies on energy, telecommunications, and other transport modes – alongside other vulnerabilities, such as supply chain fragility and potential skills shortages. Finally, there is a high risk associated with infectious diseases and health emergencies arising from contamination or infection.

Transport – Road transport subsector: Hydraulic and hydrogeological risks are assessed as medium-high. The risk associated with fires is medium. Particular attention is required regarding the structural deterioration of infrastructure in instances of inadequate maintenance. Anthropogenic threats are currently not considered significant.

Transport – Public transport subsector: Local public transport is identified as a soft target for extremist or terrorist acts. The primary vulnerabilities concern dependencies on other sectors – specifically energy – and supply chain constraints. Natural hazards are generally classified as medium or low-level.

edium or low-level.

Banking sector and financial market infrastructure: This sector exhibits medium-level vulnerabilities stemming from its dependence on ICT and telecommunications service providers, as well as the energy supply chain.

Healthcare: Critical issues are linked to natural hazards (seismic risk and, in specific regions, volcanic risk) and health emergencies caused by microbiological infections or chemical contamination. Cross-sectoral risks include dependence on energy, transport and supply chains. Furthermore, the sector faces skills shortages among qualified healthcare personnel and a heavy reliance on imports of raw materials and essential components from both EU and third countries. There is also an increasing threat from CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear) malicious activities and cyber-attacks.

Drinking water and wastewater: Significant vulnerabilities exist due to interdependencies with the energy and telecommunications sectors and the structural deterioration of infrastructure. The primary natural hazards include water scarcity for drinking water, while wastewater systems face high hydraulic, hydrogeological, and extreme meteorological risk

MISSION AND STRATEGIC OBJECTIVES

Legislative Decree No. 134 of 2024 seeks to ensure that services essential for the maintenance of vital societal functions, economic activity, public health and safety or the environment are provided without hindrance. To this end, the entities providing these services must be capable of preventing, mitigating, and absorbing disruptive physical events by responding, withstanding, and adapting to them, and ultimately restoring their operational continuity. Achieving and maintaining adequate resilience standards requires the fulfilment of specific prerequisites, which are the primary strategic objectives of this Strategy and are effectively enforced through specific policy measures grouped by objective.

The three strategic objectives are:

Objective 1 – Understanding the current sta

The three strategic objectives are:

Objective 1 – Understanding the current state of resilience of critical entities  and,

therefore, of the vital sectors of our society, also in light of cross-border and cross- sectoral dependencies and interdependencies, as a prerequisite for achieving and maintaining a high level of resilience of critical entities. This step is essential to achieve an in-depth understanding of the current state of resilience for each sector and subsector and necessary to plan effective enhancement measures.

Objective 2 – Achieving and maintaining a high level of resilience of critical entities to ensure operational continuity of essential services, even in the face of disruptive, natural, accidental, or malicious incidents.

Objective 3 – Promoting cooperation and coordination among stakeholders at national, European and international levels by facilitating the coordination of public and private initiatives that can enhance the resilience of critical infrastructure.

For the banking, financial market infrastructure, and digital infrastructure sectors, the objectives and measures outlined below shall apply within the limits and for the purposes of Article 10 of Legislative Decree No. 134 of 2024 (implementing the CER Directive), and insofar as they are compatible with other relevant EU and national provisions. The SPC coordinated a series of sectoral meetings to collect and analyse the relevant requirements, determining the most effective actions to be carried out at the institutional level. Furthermore, the process included a public consultation process, which further refined the strategic objectives and corresponding policy measures.

The resilience of the public administration is a cross-cutting priority of all the strategic  objectives.

The policy measures for implementing Objective 1, “Understanding the current state of resilience of critical entities”, are:

Defining the resilience requirements of critical entities.

Monitoring risks and vulnerabilities in critical sectors.

These measures contribute significantly to achieving strategic objective 1, as they provide the cognitive, analytical and operational instruments necessary to build a solid foundation for all subsequent resilience enhancing actions. In particular, the shared definition of resilience requirements and indicators (Measure 1.1) enables the standardisation and comparison of capacities of critical entities across different sectors. Periodic monitoring of risks and vulnerabilities (Measure 1.2), combined with the mapping of cross-border (Measure 1.3) and cross-sectoral (Measure 1.4) dependencies, provides an understanding of the systemic nature of risks; this facilitates the identification of strategic nodes and recur

Finally, the creation of a Permanent Roundtable for the health sector (Measure 1.6) introduces a replicable model of sectoral governance for operational coordination purposes and the continuous adaptation of the measures. Taken all together, the measures provide a detailed and dynamic snapshot of the state of national resilience, which is a prerequisite for any subsequent effective intervention.

DESCRIPTION OF MEASURES TO

FACILITATE COMPLIANCE WITH OBLIGATIONS BY SMALL AND MEDIUM- SIZED CRITICAL ENTITIES

Italy is characterised by an economic fabric heavily reliant on small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which account for 99.9% of all active businesses nationwide. With over 4 million SMEs, Italy ranks among the European leaders in terms of the absolute number of small and medium- sized enterprises. Within this structure, micro-enterprises (those with fewer than 10 employees) account for approximately 95% of the total, further highlighting the widespread nature of the system.

Current Support Measures

To support this vast entrepreneurial system, Italy has implemented a comp

Current Support Measures

To support this vast entrepreneurial system, Italy has implemented a comprehensive set of regulatory, fiscal and financial measures specifically targeted at SMEs. These instruments include, amongst others:

Tax credits for investments in capital goods.

Incentives for digital and technological transition.

Tax breaks for innovative start-ups.

Access to the SME Guarantee Fund, which facilitates bank loans by providing public guarantees.

These measures apply across the board to all SMEs, regardless of economic sector, legal form or geographical location, provided they meet the size criteria established by European legislation. More favourable conditions are also provided for businesses based in disadvantaged areas, those with female or youth ownership, and those investing in environmental sustainability or research and development.

Bridging the Gap: Support for SMEs with a Critical Role

To date, no support measures are specifically dedicated to SMEs that play a critical role in ensuring the continuity of essential services. This Strategy aims to bridge this gap by fostering the adoption of proportionate

ay a critical role in ensuring the continuity of essential services. This Strategy aims to bridge this gap by fostering the adoption of proportionate and targeted measures to support SMEs identified as critical entities. In this regard, conducting a detailed assessment of the potential contribution of SMEs to prevention, preparedness, and response mechanisms for disruptive events is of strategic importance.

In the current landscape of high sectoral interdependence — encompassing sectors such as energy, transport, telecommunications, healthcare, and the agri-food supply chain — a significant number of SMEs perform operational and logistical support functions that are crucial to the resilience and continuity of essential services.

It should be clarified that the identification of critical entities is designed to determine the public and private actors indispensable for the provision and maintenance of adequate levels of essential services, while also considering the availability of alternative solutions for their provision. This identification process will be conducted by defining specific significance thresholds for each sector, subsector, and, where appropriate, for specific cate

Once this process is complete and the critical entities have been designated, a verification exercise will be initiated to determine the number of SMEs falling within the scope of the Strategy. At this

stage, the types of support measures to be implemented will be assessed, potentially through structured stakeholder consultations.

In the banking, financial market infrastructure, and digital infrastructure sectors, the presence of small and medium-sized critical operators is generally negligible. The Ministry of Agriculture, Food Sovereignty and Forestry (MASAF) holds primary competence over

this sector. In defining and implementing the Strategy, the Ministry has specifically engaged the Council for Agricultural Research and Analysis of Agricultural Economics (CREA) and the Institute for Agricultural and Food Market Services (ISMEA). CREA is Italy’s leading research organisation dedicated to the agri-food supply chain; it conducts research, experimentation, and technology transfer to drive innovation and sustainable development in the agricultural and agri-food sectors. ISMEA provides information, insurance, and financial services to agricultural enterprises, while also supporting regional authorities in land consolidation and promoting generational renewal in the industry.

Irrigation water

Among the stakeholders consulted are land reclamation consortia and agricultural enterprises, represented by the National Association of Consortia for Land Management and Protection and Irrigation
